KEY MESSAGE 1: A deepening trough will result in a 
strengthening coastal low providing a shot of rain today with a 
transition to snow in the northeastern zones tonight. 

As a low pressure system approaches the region from the Ohio 
Valley, rain will continue to overspread the Commonwealth. At 5
AM this morning, much of the rain falling in central PA was 
associated with a band of 850 mb fgen forcing across the 
northern tier. Radar rainfall estimates are already near 0.50
inch locally within this band. Another spoke of stratiform 
rainfall was pivoting into southwestern PA, closer to the 
primary low pressure system. Over the next 6 hours, the low 
pressure will accelerate eastward and deepen to become sub-1000 
hPa as it passes through the Baltimore-Washington region. As it
does so, 925 hPa flow from the south across our area will back 
to become southeasterly, increasing moisture transport from the 
Chesapeake Bay into the Susquehanna Valley. This will result in 
an uptick in coverage and intensity of rain showers along and
ahead of the existing stratiform area of rainfall. MUCAPE of 
100-400 J/kg will be enough to support a few rumbles of thunder 
and heavier downpours across the Lower Susq Valley between the 
mid-morning and afternoon hours. Orographic enhancement will 
likely result in rainfall totals exceeding 1 inch between 
Schuylkill County and Sullivan County. No flooding concerns will
exist with well-below-average precipitation across the entire 
area over the past two months. SPC does highlight southeastern 
PA with a MRGL risk of severe wind and 2 pct tornado risk, just 
to the east of Lancaster County, where hodographs are a bit more
curved. 

Cold air will wrap in on the back side of the storm this evening.
While the main area of precip will have already pulled away 
from much of central PA, fgen forcing supports a more 
persistent comma head lingering across northeast zones, in 
particular Sullivan and Tioga Counties, where steady rain is 
likely to transition to snow around or shortly after sunset. The
most likely scenario at this point is a coating-2" of snow 
tonight into Friday, with locally higher amounts of 2.0-3.5" 
possible in the higher terrain of eastern Sullivan and eastern 
Tioga counties. Ensemble guidance also suggests a 1-in-10 chance
of snowfall amounts exceeding 3 inches in the higher terrain of
Schuylkill County, including along I-81, so this potential will
have to be monitored. Given the antecedent warm ground, 
accumulations are likely to be slushy with higher amounts on 
grassy surfaces. Motorists are urged to use extra caution as 
this is the first snowfall of the season.

------------------------------------------------------------------

KEY MESSAGE 2: Northwesterly flow brings much cooler 
temperatures this weekend, with lake-enhanced snow showers 
continuing through the weekend.

Cooler temperatures and breezy northwesterly winds will take 
hold of the region as the area of low pressure shifts east 
towards the New England Coast. Wind gusts in the 25-35 mph range
are likely from tonight through the weekend, strongest tonight 
into Friday. By sunrise on Friday, most guidance shows 
stratiform precip pulling away and north-south oriented lake 
effect streamer bands will likely be in its wake. It should be 
noted, however, that a few model runs do show the stratiform 
comma head snowfall lingering longer across eastern PA, but 
rates would be light enough and sfc temps warm enough to 
preclude any significant impacts. At this time, snowfall does 
appear to be the dominant precipitation type across the 
I-80/I-99 corridor and north/west, with a mix or plain rain to 
the south and east. The lake effect and upslope snow on the back
side of this system is expected to produce a coating to one 
inch of snow across the Laurels and the northwest mountains with
localized amounts pushing closer to two inches in the highest 
elevations and in areas of locally persistent banding.

Chances for precipitation begin to decrease later Sunday as a 
subsidence inversion builds in with approaching high pressure. A
slight warming trend emerges into the beginning of next week, 
with temperatures trending closer to climatological averages by 
Tuesday.
